articles.title: PM Modi Inaugurates India's First LED Dome Planetarium in Mysuru | DD News
articles.content: 1 hour ago | India's First LED Dome Planetarium in Mysuru | PM Modi Inaugurates India's First LED Dome Planetarium | Prime Minister Narendra Modi PM Modi Inaugurates India’s First LED Dome Planetarium in Mysuru Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday inaugurated COSMOS-Mysuru Planetarium, India’s first LED dome planetarium, in Mysuru, Karnataka, and described it as a significant addition to the country’s scientific and educational infrastructure. Addressing the gathering, PM Modi greeted the people in Kannada and expressed happiness over returning to Mysuru to dedicate the planetarium to the nation, months after inaugurating the Viveka Smaraka. Drawing a parallel between the two landmarks, he said that while the Viveka Smaraka encourages introspection and spiritual pursuits, the COSMOS Planetarium inspires people to explore the mysteries of the universe. “This is an example of the fact that in India, the traditions of spirituality and science have always moved forward together,” he said. Recalling India’s rich astronomical heritage, the Prime Minister highlighted the contributions of ancient Indian scholars, including Aryabhata, Varahamihira, Bhaskaracharya and Nilakantha Somayaji, who studied celestial movements, developed calendars and calculated solar and lunar eclipses without access to modern instruments and technology. PM Modi also highlighted Mysuru’s contribution to the country’s educational and scientific development, recalling the establishment of the University of Mysore under Maharaja Nalwadi Krishnaraja Wadiyar and the Wadiyar royal family’s role in laying the foundation of the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru. He said the new planetarium would add another chapter to Mysuru’s legacy of promoting knowledge and scientific learning. Describing his experience of watching a show inside the LED dome as wonderful, he congratulated the institutions and officials involved in the project, including the Indian Institute of Astrophysics and the University of Mysore. Tracing India’s scientific progress, PM Modi referred to the evolution of the national slogan from ‘Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan’ to ‘Jai Vigyan’, introduced by former Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee, and subsequently to ‘Jai Anusandhan’, which he said reflects India’s research and innovation ambitions. Highlighting the achievements of Indian students in international science competitions, he recalled the country’s performance at the International Olympiad on Astronomy and Astrophysics. Five Indian students participated in this year’s edition in Vietnam, with four winning gold medals and one securing silver. He also cited the achievements of young Indians at international Olympiads in Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry and Biology, saying that students could achieve extraordinary results when provided with access to quality education, technology, resources and institutional support. The COSMOS Planetarium, he said, would help nurture their scientific ambitions. Emphasising the need to keep pace with rapid technological advancements, the Prime Minister outlined India’s progress in astronomy, astrophysics and space exploration over the past decade. He cited the Chandrayaan-3 mission, which made India the first country to land near the Moon’s south pole, and the launch of Aditya-L1, India’s first space-based solar observatory. articles.title: G Kishan Reddy Launches Critical Minerals Research Hub And … - The Open Press
articles.content: Politics G Kishan Reddy Launches Critical Minerals Research Hub And India's First VR Mine Training Facility At IIT Dhanbad Union Minister for Coal and Mines G Kishan Reddy on Thursday inaugurated a Centre of Excellence for Critical Minerals and India's first Virtual Reality-based mine simulator at the Indian Institute of… Published By : Politics Desk , Dhanbad Last Updated: November 13, 2026, 09:53 IST Union Minister for Coal and Mines G Kishan Reddy speaks at IIT (ISM) Dhanbad, where he inaugurated a Centre of Excellence for Critical Minerals and a VR mine simulator on Thursday. Union Minister for Coal and Mines G Kishan Reddy on Thursday inaugurated a Centre of Excellence for Critical Minerals and India's first Virtual Reality-based mine simulator at the Indian Institute of Technology (ISM) in Dhanbad, in a push to bring advanced research and modern training into the mining sector. The Centre of Excellence has been established under the National Critical Minerals Mission and is envisioned as a national platform for advanced research and scalable industry solutions. Alongside the research hub, the Minister inaugurated India's first Virtual Reality Mine Simulator for coal mining operations, marking a significant step toward technology-led transformation of India's mining sector. A national platform for critical minerals Critical minerals are essential for electric vehicles, renewable energy systems, electronics and defence manufacturing, and securing their supply has become a strategic priority for India as it builds clean energy and high-technology industries. The new centre at Dhanbad will work on advanced research and solutions that industry can adopt at scale, connecting laboratory work with the practical needs of mining and mineral processing. Global and domestic partnerships The centre will collaborate with leading international academic institutions such as the University of Cambridge and St Petersburg University, strengthening its global research ecosystem. It will also receive infrastructure and technical support from IIT Gandhinagar, IIT (BHU) Varanasi and CPI (UK), linking Dhanbad's mining expertise with research institutions across India and abroad. Training miners in virtual reality The VR mine simulator lets trainees practise coal mining operations in an immersive virtual environment, building skills and familiarity with mining work without the risks of underground operations. Virtual training of this kind is increasingly used around the world to prepare workers for hazardous industries safely. IIT (ISM) Dhanbad is one of India's oldest mining schools, and the new facilities add research and training capacity to an institution at the heart of the country's coal belt. The inaugurations mark a step toward a mining sector built on research, technology and global collaboration, with Dhanbad hosting work that connects India's mineral future to its mining heritage. The facility has been built as a centre for cosmology education and research training, according to a report by Prajavani – Mysuru. The inauguration places a new science and education facility within Mysuru’s institutional and cultural landscape. The planetarium is intended to support learning and training related to cosmology, while its LED curved-dome format distinguishes it from conventional planetarium infrastructure described in the report. Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman briefed the Prime Minister about the planetarium during the inauguration. The event was attended by Karnataka Governor Sudha Yadav, Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar and Higher Education Minister Basavaraj Rayareddy, along with other officials, Prajavani reported. The facility has been named Cosmos Mysore and is located near Chamundi Hill, one of the city’s most prominent geographical and cultural landmarks. Its location connects a science-oriented public institution with an area that is already associated with Mysuru’s visitor economy and civic identity. The supplied report, however, does not provide details on the project’s cost, construction timeline, seating capacity, programming schedule or expected visitor numbers. The planetarium’s stated focus on cosmology education and research training gives it a role beyond a one-time public exhibition. Such facilities can function as platforms for structured learning and scientific engagement, but the available report does not specify the academic institutions, research organisations or administrative agencies that will operate Cosmos Mysore. The inauguration also brings attention to the importance of specialised educational infrastructure outside India’s largest metropolitan centres. Mysuru already has a strong association with education and heritage, and the new facility adds a science and astronomy-oriented institution to that urban profile. The report does not establish whether the planetarium will be open to schools, colleges, researchers or the general public, or whether admission and outreach arrangements have been announced. The event was attended by senior Union and Karnataka government representatives, indicating official recognition of the facility’s education and research objectives. Further information on its operating model, public access, educational partnerships and regular programming will determine how Cosmos Mysore functions after the inauguration. articles.title: Mysuru Planetarium Opens With India's First LED Dome Experience
articles.content: Home Breaking News Mysuru Planetarium Opens With India’s First LED Dome Experience Breaking News Mysuru Planetarium Opens With India’s First LED Dome Experience By Ayesha Siddiqui November 13, 2026 0 Copy URL Facebook Linkedin X WhatsApp Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the Cosmos-Mysore planetarium at the foothills of Chamundi Hill on Friday, opening a ₹115-crore facility designed for cosmology education, research training and immersive visualisation of space. The centre has been described as India’s first LED curved-dome planetarium. Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman briefed the Prime Minister about the facility during the inauguration. After the ceremony, Modi viewed space-related displays from inside the sky theatre. Karnataka Governor Sudha Yadav, Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar and Higher Education Minister Basavaraj Rayareddy were among those present. The planetarium’s main attraction is a 15-metre-diameter sky theatre with 160 seats. Its LED dome is installed at a 15-degree angle to create an immersive viewing experience. Unlike conventional systems that use projectors, the facility uses densely arranged LED panels on the inner surface of the dome to emit light directly. The display system has a resolution of 42 megapixels across a 353.4-square-metre surface. According to the source report, this capacity is higher than standard true 8K resolution. The curved surface can display continuous visuals without interruptions across the dome, allowing audiences to view space-related films and simulations across the entire field of vision. The system is supported by high-capacity computing infrastructure with 14 graphics processing units and advanced Sky Explorer software. The combination is intended to produce high-resolution and bright visuals for visitors. The facility can also connect with remote locations such as Hanle, enabling it to provide an experience based on the real night sky, according to the report. The planetarium is intended for uses beyond public entertainment. Its stated applications include astronomy education, immersive visual experiences, data visualisation and teaching across different areas of science. This places the facility within Mysuru’s broader educational and cultural infrastructure, while its location near Chamundi Hill adds a major public destination to the city’s visitor landscape. The inauguration marks the opening of a specialised facility whose operations will combine public engagement with educational and research-oriented programming. The centre’s LED dome, sky theatre and remote-sky connectivity are the principal features identified in the source report. articles.title: Modi inaugurates India's first LED Dome Planetarium in Mysuru, urges students to explore science
articles.content: MAYSURU: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday said the state-of-the-art COSMOS Planetarium in Mysuru would inspire young minds to explore the mysteries of the universe and contribute to India's growing scientific achievements. Speaking after dedicating COSMOS, India's first LED Dome Planetarium, to the nation, Modi said the facility would add a new chapter to India's scientific journey and provide students and researchers with opportunities to develop scientific curiosity and pursue new discoveries. Drawing a parallel between the Viveka Smaraka, which was inaugurated by him in Mysuru recently, and COSMOS Planetarium, Modi said the two institutions conveyed a profound message about India's traditions of spirituality and science. While Viveka Smaraka inspired people to look within and seek spiritual knowledge, COSMOS encouraged them to look towards the skies and understand the vast universe. "India's traditions of spirituality and science have always progressed together," he said, recalling the contributions of ancient Indian astronomers such as Aryabhata, Varahamihira, Bhaskaracharya and Neelakantha Somayaji, who made significant discoveries and complex calculations without access to modern instruments and technology. Speaking about Mysuru's legacy of promoting education and research, Modi recalled that the University of Mysore was established during the reign of Nalwadi Krishnaraja Wadiyar and that the Wadiyar family played an important role in laying the foundation for the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru. These institutions had provided opportunities for generations of students and researchers, he said. Congratulating the Indian Institute of Astrophysics, the University of Mysore, various government departments and everyone associated with the project, Modi described COSMOS as an extraordinary experience, noting that he had the opportunity to watch a show at the planetarium. Referring to India's achievements in international science competitions, the Prime Minister said five Indian students participated in the International Olympiad on Astronomy and Astrophysics held in Vietnam this year, with four winning gold medals and one securing a silver medal. Indian students had also achieved record success in international Olympiads in mathematics, physics, chemistry and biology, winning gold or silver medals, he said. "When young people are provided with opportunities, resources, technology, tools and institutional support, they demonstrate their ability to achieve remarkable milestones," Modi said, adding that COSMOS would play an important role in shaping their dreams. Highlighting India's progress in space exploration over the past decade, he cited the successful Chandrayaan-3 mission, which made India the first country to land near the Moon's south polar region, and Aditya-L1, the country's first space-based solar observatory. India had also become the fourth country to demonstrate space docking and undocking capabilities, he said. He referred to an Indian astronaut's visit to the International Space Station and said the experience and experiments conducted during the mission would contribute to India's human spaceflight programme, Gaganyaan. Modi said the opening up of the space sector had created new opportunities for private companies and start-ups, enabling young entrepreneurs to develop rockets, launch satellites and undertake activities that were previously unprecedented in India. articles.title: India's first day-care bilateral hip replacement performed at Delhi hospital - ThePrint
articles.content: Support our Journalism Depth, context and analysis Subscribe Home India India's first day-care bilateral hip replacement performed at Delhi hospital India India’s first day-care bilateral hip replacement performed at Delhi hospital PTI 13 November, 2026 06:53 pm IST Follow Us: Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Email Copy Link Stay updated with ThePrint: Preferred Source Google Discover New Delhi, Nov 13 (PTI) Doctors at a private hospital in south Delhi have performed what they described as India’s first day-care bilateral total hip replacement using Smart AI Navigation technology, with a 40-year-old patient from Myanmar discharged on the same day. The procedure, in which both hip joints were replaced in a single surgical session, was performed at Max Super Speciality Hospital, Saket, by a team led by Dr Sujoy Bhattacharjee, Chairman and Chief of the hospital’s Institute of Robotic Joint Replacement. The patient, Juya Mani, was suffering from avascular necrosis of both hips, a condition in which reduced blood supply causes bone tissue to deteriorate. He had experienced pain for several years, which had worsened in recent months and increasingly restricted his ability to walk, according to the hospital. Show Full Article The surgery took approximately three-and-a-half hours. The patient was mobilised under medical supervision within four hours of being shifted to the recovery room and discharged after meeting the required clinical and functional criteria. Both hips were replaced using uncemented implants from the Meril Libertas Hip Replacement System, the hospital said. Bilateral hip replacement patients generally require hospitalisation for several days for monitoring, pain management and rehabilitation. However, a combination of navigation-assisted surgery, preoperative planning and an enhanced recovery protocol enabled the team to mobilise the patient early and facilitate same-day discharge. “Replacing both hips in one sitting normally means a longer hospital stay for monitoring and rehabilitation. Smart AI Navigation gave us precise implant positioning and alignment, and with careful planning and a structured recovery protocol we were able to mobilise the patient early and send him home safely the same day,” Bhattacharjee said. He said the procedure demonstrated that same-day discharge was possible even after bilateral hip replacement in carefully selected patients. Navigation-assisted hip replacement uses surgical planning and computer guidance to help surgeons position implants according to a patient’s anatomy, while the surgeon retains control of the procedure, the hospital said. Bilateral hip replacement is generally recommended for patients with advanced disease affecting both hips, including severe osteoarthritis and avascular necrosis. Performing both replacements in one sitting avoids a second operation and anaesthesia, while allowing the patient to undergo a single period of rehabilitation, it added. articles.title: Karnataka CM Demands Action On Mekedatu, Kasturirangan Report - Rediff.com
articles.content: Karnataka Chief Minister D K Shivakumar pressed the Centre on critical issues including the Mekedatu project, the Kasturirangan report, and CSR alignment for education, while also celebrating the inauguration of the CoSMOS facility in Mysuru. Karnataka Chief Minister D K Shivakumar on Friday urged the Centre to expedite the statutory clearances for the Mekedatu balancing reservoir project and withdraw the recommendations of the Kasturirangan report on the Western Ghats. He asked the Centre to align corporate social responsibility (CSR) initiatives with the state's guidelines to help upgrade 1,000 government schools into Karnataka Public Schools. Shivakumar placed the three demands while addressing the inauguration of CoSMOS (Centre of Space and Modern Optical Sciences) in Mysuru, in the presence of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. He underscored the need for cooperation between the Union and state governments to address critical developmental challenges. Referring to proposed Mekedatu dam, he said the Supreme Court had already delivered its verdict, and the legal position was settled. "Sir, you just saw the dam on the Cauvery. The Supreme Court has delivered a clear verdict to all of us that Mekedatu has to be built in Karnataka, and no one can stop it. We want you to help us legally," he said. He urged the Centre to grant the final statutory clearances so that the drinking water project could proceed without further delay. "Let us all work together. The Cauvery, which flows through this river basin, helps Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, Kerala, Bengaluru and different regions. So, we want you to help us. This is a balancing reservoir for drinking water, which will help Tamil Nadu as well," he claimed. Mekedatu is a balancing reservoir project across the Cauvery near Kanakapura, Shivakumar's home town. It aims to meet the drinking water needs of Bengaluru and act as a buffer to ensure adequate water for Tamil Nadu during droughts. Tamil Nadu opposes the project, saying it would hurt its farmers. On the Western Ghats, Shivakumar said the Karnataka legislature had unanimously passed a resolution opposing the Kasturirangan report's recommendations after extensive public consultations across the affected regions. "We held consultations and passed a resolution. We want a unanimous resolution opposing the Kasturirangan report, and we want you to help us on this," he told the PM. He urged the Centre to respect the sentiments of the people of the region and withdraw the recommendations to protect local livelihoods. The Centre issued the seventh draft notification, based on the Kasturirangan report, on July 27, 2026, allowing 60 days for objections. It proposes to declare 56,000 sq km across six states as an Ecologically Sensitive Area (ESA). The state has repeatedly rejected the Centre's draft notifications. In Karnataka, 20,668 sq km covering 33 taluks and 1,449 villages in 10 districts (Belagavi, Chamarajanagar, Chikkamagaluru, Kodagu, Hassan, Uttara Kannada, Dakshina Kannada, Mysuru, Shivamogga and Udupi) would fall under the ESA. articles.title: India's First LED Dome Planetarium in Mysuru to Open Today, PM Modi to Inaugurate COSMOS
articles.content: India India's First LED Dome Planetarium in Mysuru to Open Today, PM Modi to Inaugurate COSMOS India's science education landscape gets a dazzling upgrade on 13 November 2026, when Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurates the COSMOS-Mysuru Planetarium, a facility unlike any other in the countr… Published By : India Desk , Mysuru, Karnataka Last Updated: November 13, 2026, 06:09 IST The COSMOS-Mysuru planetarium in Karnataka, India's first LED dome planetarium, which Prime Minister Narendra Modi is scheduled to inaugurate on 13 November 2026. India's science education landscape gets a dazzling upgrade on 13 November 2026, when Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurates the COSMOS-Mysuru Planetarium, a facility unlike any other in the country, built not with projectors and passive screens, but with 4.2 crore individual LEDs stitched across a living dome. Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman shared the announcement on 12 November 2026, noting that the project received Rs 5 crore in funding through her own MPLADS contribution. The planetarium has been built by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics. A dome that is the display Built by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics, COSMOS-Mysuru is India's first LED Dome planetarium, and the distinction matters. Conventional planetariums fire images onto a passive dome using a projector at the centre. Here, the dome itself is the display: a 15-metre tilted dome made up of around 6,150 panels, each studded with LEDs that can be controlled in real time. The result is an immersive visual environment that can shift, respond and adapt in ways no projector-based setup can match. That real-time controllability opens entirely new possibilities for astronomy education, from live celestial simulations to interactive shows that respond to audience questions. It is a leap in the same direction that high-end planetariums in Europe and Japan have pursued, now arriving in Mysuru, Karnataka. MPLADS funding for science The Members of Parliament Local Area Development Scheme allows sitting MPs to recommend development works in their constituencies, with an annual entitlement currently set at Rs 5 crore per year. Sitharaman, a Rajya Sabha member from Karnataka, channelled that allocation toward the COSMOS project. The funding choice redirects a discretionary fund often associated with roads and drains toward cutting-edge science infrastructure, and it signals how such allocations can be used to build lasting public assets for education. The Indian Institute of Astrophysics, headquartered in Bengaluru with field stations across southern India, is one of India's premier astronomy research bodies. Its decision to build COSMOS-Mysuru reflects a broader mandate to bridge research and public science communication, and COSMOS is its most ambitious public-facing project yet. Shows in three languages The planetarium's Sky Theatre will screen professionally produced astronomy programmes for the public. Alongside those, an in-house film will explore the deep historical connection between Mysuru and astronomy, a nod to the region's rich heritage as a centre of scientific patronage under the Wadiyar dynasty. Shows will run in Kannada, English and Hindi, ensuring the facility serves local communities as much as visiting students and tourists. That trilingual offering signals...

articles.title: PM Modi Inaugurates India's First LED Dome Planetarium in Mysuru - Deccan Chronicle
articles.content: Mysuru: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday inaugurated COSMOS-Mysuru Planetarium, India's first LED dome planetarium, at the University of Mysore campus, marking a new addition to Karnataka's scientific and educational infrastructure. Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, Karnataka Chief Minister DK Shivakumar and other dignitaries were present at the inaugural ceremony. Built by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA), COSMOS-Mysuru has been envisaged as an astronomy education, research and training centre. Located at the foothills of Chamundi Hills, the facility aims to promote scientific curiosity and make astronomy more accessible to students and the public. The state-of-the-art facility features a 15-metre tilted dome comprising around 6,150 panels with 4.2 crore individual LEDs. Unlike conventional planetariums that use projectors to display images on a passive dome, its LED panels can be controlled in real time, offering an immersive visual experience and new possibilities for astronomy education. The Sky Theatre will showcase professionally produced astronomy programmes, along with an in-house film exploring the connection between the history of Mysuru and astronomy. The shows will be available in Kannada, English and Hindi. Addressing the inaugural ceremony, Sitharaman described COSMOS-Mysuru as an important addition to the city's longstanding tradition of learning and scholarship, while highlighting its contribution to astronomy education and scientific research. "Today, the Hon'ble Prime Minister dedicates the COSMOS Planetarium, a centre for cosmology education, research and training. Here in Mysuru, with its long tradition of learning and scholarship, we now welcome a new institution devoted to understanding the universe," she said. The Union Finance Minister thanked the Governor, the Chief Minister, the Karnataka government and the Mysuru district administration for their support and cooperation in establishing the facility. She also welcomed students and teachers from Mysuru schools who attended the ceremony. Sitharaman credited the scientists, engineers, architects and construction teams for making the centre possible, while highlighting Karnataka's contribution to India's scientific development. "This achievement also belongs to the scientists, engineers, architects and construction teams who have made this centre possible. Karnataka's contribution to science has deep roots. It has a long tradition of supporting science and education and has played a crucial role in building India's scientific capabilities," she said. Highlighting Karnataka's growing presence in emerging technology sectors, she said the state had established a strong position in information technology, aerospace, biotechnology and space technology, supported by research institutions, startups and MSMEs. "With COSMOS in Mysuru, we add another feature to its cap. India's first LED dome planetarium brings many important benefits. COSMOS makes astronomy accessible through an immersive learning experience. It helps children understand stars and planets and encourages them to ask questions," Sitharaman said.

articles.title: IIM Bangalore gets IGBC Platinum Green Campus certification - Careers360 News
articles.content: Soumi Roy | November 13, 2026 | 01:29 PM IST | 2 mins read IIMB has earned distinction under the IGBC Green Campus Rating System Version 1.0, recognising its initiatives in energy efficiency, water conservation, renewable energy and sustainable campus management. The Indian Institute of Management Bangalore (IIMB) has received Platinum certification under the Indian Green Building Council’s (IGBC) Green Campus Rating System Version 1.0, becoming the first educational institution in India to earn the distinction under this framework. The certification reflects IIM Bangalore’s campus-wide sustainability measures, including energy efficiency, water conservation, renewable energy use, waste management, occupant wellbeing and responsible resource utilisation. The IIM Bangalore campus , designed by BV Doshi, an architect and Pritzker Prize laureate, is known for its climate-responsive architecture. Its interconnected courtyards, shaded walkways and emphasis on natural light and ventilation help reduce dependence on artificial lighting and cooling. The campus also has extensive green areas that support biodiversity. Also read CAT 2026: In a first, IIM Indore to use AI-based face recognition along with admit card check at exam centres IIMB is among only five facilities in India to have received Platinum status under the IGBC rating system's Version 1.0. The other recipients are Odisha Lok Bhavan in Bhubaneswar, SP Infocity in Pune, IndianOil Corporation's campus in Faridabad and Schindler's campus in Pune. Water management is a key part of the institute's sustainability initiatives. Its campus has rainwater harvesting, storage and groundwater recharge facilities. A 500 kilolitres per day (KLD) sewage treatment plant processes all wastewater generated on campus, with treated water reused for flushing and landscaping. The institute has installed 350 kilowatt-peak (kWp) of rooftop solar capacity and proposed an additional 150 kWp. It is also exploring renewable energy sourcing from off-campus facilities. Electric buggies and an electric bus have been introduced for internal transport, which can be fast-charged. Also read IIM Bangalore reports 100% PGP, PGPBA summer placements; Rs 2 lakh median stipend, Accenture top recruiters IIMB follows waste segregation, treats organic waste on campus and sends dry waste for recycling through authorised vendors. Its responsible procurement practices include the use of recycled paper, environmentally friendly housekeeping products, organic fertilisers and biodegradable waste liners. The institute also checks for indoor air quality in classrooms to support healthier learning and working conditions. IIMB has also conducted greenhouse gas assessments and other studies to identify measures for reducing its environmental footprint. These initiatives will support its broader ambition of achieving Net Zero emissions. articles.title: What is COSMOS-Mysuru? How India's first LED dome planetarium will help students explore space
articles.content: Edited By : Aiswarya Venugopal Last Updated: 13 Nov 2026, 05:19 pm IST 3 min Share Follow us on Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurates COSMOS-Mysuru, India's first LED dome planetarium. Know how its 8K technology works and how it will support astronomy education. ❎ India's first LED dome planetarium in Mysuru MYSURU: Imagine looking up at the night sky and seeing planets, stars, distant galaxies and other celestial phenomena spread across an entire dome above you. Now imagine that the images are not being projected from a machine but are displayed directly by millions of tiny LED lights. That is the technology behind COSMOS-Mysuru, India's first LED dome planetarium, inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday. To advertise here, Contact Us Developed by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA), the Cosmology Education and Research Training Centre is located on the University of Mysore campus at the foothills of Chamundi Hills. It combines an advanced planetarium with facilities for astronomy education, data analysis and research training. How is an LED dome planetarium different? Most conventional planetariums use a projector to cast images and videos onto the inside of a dome. The dome itself acts as a passive surface on which the visuals appear. COSMOS-Mysuru uses a different system. Its dome is made up of LED panels that display images directly, eliminating the need for a conventional projection system. The 15-metre dome is tilted and consists of around 6,150 panels containing approximately 4.2 crore individual LEDs. The system offers 8K resolution and can be controlled through a computer system to display high-resolution visuals across the dome. According to the Indian Institute of Astrophysics, the technology offers better contrast and a wider range of colours. It also creates possibilities for displaying live astronomical data, telescope observations and scientific visualisations. How will it help students and the public? The technology is expected to make astronomy easier to understand by allowing audiences to explore the universe through immersive visual presentations. Instead of learning about planets, stars and other celestial objects only through textbooks or conventional classroom diagrams, students can experience visual representations of astronomical phenomena across the dome. The facility is also designed to go beyond regular planetarium shows. Its planned activities include academic workshops, data-analysis programmes and training for students and teachers. The LED dome can also be used as a teaching tool to explain astronomical observations and scientific concepts. The institute's plans include using the facility to display data from Indian telescopes and introduce students to the process of analysing astronomical information. The centre will also have exhibition halls, a museum featuring astronomy models and artefacts, lecture halls, training facilities and interactive outdoor science exhibits. Telescope facilities for viewing the Sun and stars are also part of the project. Three years of groundwork in astronomy education The planetarium is the culmination of a three-year astronomy education and outreach programme conducted by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics in Mysuru and surrounding rural areas. The Sky Theatre will screen professionally produced astronomy programmes, along with an in-house film exploring the connection between the history of Mysuru and astronomy. The shows will be available in Kannada, English and Hindi. The centre will also house exhibition halls, a museum featuring astronomy models and artefacts, a lecture hall, a training centre and interactive outdoor exhibits. The activities of COSMOS-Mysuru will complement the research undertaken by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics, including the operation of multi-wavelength telescope facilities across India and in space, the development of future astronomical facilities and national-level outreach programmes.

articles.title: Manipur boxer Lairenlakpam Ambekar Meetei makes history with India's first Youth Olympics gold
articles.content: News Manipur Manipur boxer Lairenlakpam Ambekar Meetei makes history with India's first Youth Olympics gold Manipur boxer Lairenlakpam Ambekar Meetei makes history with India's first Youth Olympics gold Lairenlakpam Ambekar Meetei defeated Ireland's Jubani Kristian 3-2 in the men's 50kg final. His victory delivered India's first Youth Olympics boxing gold and lifted the medal tally to nine. The victory not only marked a landmark moment for Indian boxing but also secured the country's first gold medal at the ongoing edition of the Games, taking India's overall medal tally to nine, the Boxing Federation of India (BFI) said in a press note. India had never won a boxing gold at the Youth Olympic Games before Ambekar Meetei's triumph. The country now has one gold, three silver and five bronze medals, placing it ninth in the overall standings. India could add another gold to its tally later on Thursday, with Gunjan set to compete in the women's boxing final at 10.30 pm IST. She entered the title clash after defeating Great Britain's Lily Bassett 4-1 in the semi-finals. Ambekar Meetei had also delivered a dominant performance in the last-four stage, defeating Colombia's Izzon Jeffrey Galea Arevalo 5-0 to book his place in the final. India's medal haul at Dakar has come across several disciplines, including athletics, wrestling, judo, badminton, swimming and wushu. In athletics, Shourya Ambure won bronze in the women's 100m hurdles with a personal best of 13.59 seconds, becoming the first Indian woman to win an athletics medal at the Youth Olympic Games. Taniya secured silver in the women's 75kg wrestling category, giving India its first-ever youth wrestling medal at the competition. She lost 1-2 to China's Min Zhao, the 2025 U17 World Wrestling Championships gold medallist in the 69kg category, in the final. Khushbu Rajakbhai Darjada in women's 63kg judo and Tanvi Patri in badminton also won silver medals. Swimming added three medals to India's tally. Dhinidhi Desinghu claimed bronze in both the women's 100m and 200m freestyle events, becoming the first Indian athlete to win multiple medals at a single edition of the Youth Olympic Games. Tirthank Pegu also secured bronze in the men's 200m butterfly, becoming the first Indian male swimmer to win a medal at the event. Rajkumari Lanchenbi Chanu completed India's medal tally in wushu with a bronze in the women's changquan combined event. articles.title: India's Journey of Discovery and Innovation in Space - Rising Kashmir
articles.content: Opinion India's Journey of Discovery and Innovation in Space The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) has developed rockets and satellites that support communication, navigation, weather forecasting and early warnings of natural disasters ER. SUHAIB BAKSHI 13 Nov 2026 02:18 IST Follow Us BEYOND THE SKY Space has always inspired human curiosity. From observing the stars to developing spacecraft, generations have sought to understand the universe and humanity's place within it. Today, advances in scientific research and technology are making it possible to explore space in ways once considered beyond reach. India is now an active part of this wider journey of discovery, with its space programme entering an important new phase. India's early space research began with modest facilities and ambitious scientific goals. On 21 November 1963, a research rocket carrying instruments to study the upper atmosphere was launched from Thumba in Kerala. India's first indigenous sounding rocket followed in 1967. Such rockets carry scientific instruments into the atmosphere to collect information. These early initiatives helped develop the knowledge and experience needed for a long-term space programme. Vikram Sarabhai, recognised as the father of India's space programme, believed that space technology could help address practical needs on Earth. His vision placed importance on communication, education, weather forecasting and the responsible use of scientific knowledge. That approach continues to influence the development of space technology. The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) has developed rockets and satellites that support communication, navigation, weather forecasting and early warnings of natural disasters. Its scientific missions have also contributed to the understanding of the Moon, Mars and the Sun. Chandrayaan-3 reached the Moon's southern high-latitude region on 23 August 2023, and its Pragyan rover conducted scientific studies on the lunar surface. Mangalyaan entered Mars orbit in September 2014, while Aditya-L1 reached its observing position in January 2024 to study the Sun. The space sector is also seeing growing participation from private Indian companies, which are contributing to the development of launch vehicles, satellites, engines and space-based services. This wider participation is creating opportunities for engineers, scientists, researchers and young entrepreneurs. Among the companies working in this field is Skyroot Aerospace, founded in Hyderabad in 2018. In November 2022, its Vikram-S rocket completed a suborbital test flight, demonstrating its rocket technology without placing a satellite into orbit. On 18 July 2026, the company's Vikram-1 made its maiden orbital launch, placing two satellites, Skyroot's SCOPE and Grahaa Space's SOLARAS S3, into low Earth orbit. An orbital launch, on the other hand, gives a satellite the speed and direction needed to continue travelling around Earth. These missions marked important stages in the development of Skyroot's launch vehicles. Agnikul Cosmos, based in Chennai, is developing small rockets designed to carry satellites. In May 2024, it tested Agnibaan SOrTeD using a single-piece engine made through 3D printing, a process in which an object is built layer by layer from a digital design. The flight was a suborbital technology test. Such experiments demonstrate how research, engineering and careful testing help turn ideas...
